reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: HAE causes recurrent, non-pruritic, non-pitting angioedema without urticaria, distinguishing it from mast-cell (histamine)-driven allergic angioedema
Attacks are bradykinin-mediated, so they do not respond to antihistamines, corticosteroids, or adrenaline, which is a key clue when swelling fails to improve with standard allergy treatment
Recurrent painful abdominal attacks from bowel-wall oedema can mimic a surgical abdomen and lead to unnecessary operations
Laryngeal involvement is the feared complication because progressive upper-airway oedema can cause asphyxiation and death
Attacks are commonly triggered by trauma (including dental and surgical procedures), infection, emotional stress, and oestrogens, and many begin in childhood or adolescence
Most cases are due to deficient (type 1) or dysfunctional (type 2) C1 inhibitor; a subgroup has normal C1 inhibitor with mutations such as in factor XII, so functional testing matters
A low C4 level is a useful screening abnormality; diagnosis is confirmed with C1-inhibitor antigenic level and function, and a low C1q helps identify acquired rather than hereditary disease
Management has three arms: treatment of acute attacks, short-term prophylaxis before triggering procedures, and long-term prophylaxis to reduce attack frequency

Targeted therapies act on the bradykinin pathway, including C1-inhibitor replacement, a bradykinin B2-receptor antagonist, and a plasma kallikrein inhibitor; ACE inhibitors and oestrogen-containing agents should be avoided as they worsen disease
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary angioedema most often results from autosomal dominant deficiency or dysfunction of C1 inhibitor (SERPING1 mutations). C1 inhibitor normally restrains the contact (kallikrein-kinin), complement, and fibrinolytic systems. Its deficiency permits unchecked activation of plasma kallikrein, which cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to generate excess bradykinin. Bradykinin acting on B2 receptors increases vascular permeability, producing the characteristic submucosal and subcutaneous oedema. A minority of patients have HAE with normal C1 inhibitor caused by mutations that enhance contact-system activation (e.g. factor XII, plasminogen, angiopoietin-1). Because the mechanism is kinin- rather than histamine-driven, mast-cell-directed therapies are ineffective.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency (often with lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease, low C1q)
Allergic/histaminergic angioedema with or without urticaria
Superior vena cava obstruction or localised infection causing facial swelling
additionalInvestigations: Serum C4 level as an initial screen (typically low during and between attacks)
C1-inhibitor antigenic concentration and functional activity
C1q level to help distinguish acquired from hereditary disease
Genetic testing (e.g. SERPING1, factor XII) in atypical or normal-C1-inhibitor cases
Family history assessment and screening of at-risk relatives
redFlags: Laryngeal or tongue swelling, voice change, stridor, or difficulty swallowing indicating life-threatening airway obstruction requiring urgent bradykinin-targeted therapy and airway management
Severe abdominal attacks risking misdiagnosis as an acute surgical abdomen
Swelling unresponsive to adrenaline, antihistamines, and corticosteroids
Rapid progression of facial or oropharyngeal oedema, particularly after dental or surgical procedures
reference.prognosis: With modern on-demand and prophylactic therapy targeting the bradykinin pathway, most patients achieve good disease control and near-normal life expectancy. Untreated or unrecognised laryngeal attacks, however, carry a substantial risk of death from asphyxiation.
pitfalls: Treating attacks as allergic and relying on antihistamines, steroids, or adrenaline, which are ineffective
Failing to recognise abdominal attacks and proceeding to unnecessary surgery
Prescribing ACE inhibitors or oestrogen-containing contraceptives, which precipitate attacks
Omitting short-term prophylaxis before dental, surgical, or airway procedures
